The court has continued to uphold the fighting words doctrine but also steadily narrowed the grounds on which fighting words are held to apply. In a notable case, the court overturned a statute prohibiting flag-burning and verbally abusing the flag, holding that mere offensiveness does not qualify as "fighting words."

Additionally, in another significant ruling, the court overturned a statute prohibiting speech or symbolic expression that "arouses anger, alarm or resentment in others on the basis of race, color, creed, religion or gender" on the grounds that, even if the specific statute was limited to fighting words, it was unconstitutionally content-based and viewpoint-based because of the limitation to race-/religion-/sex-based fighting words.

Furthermore, in a recent case, a dissenting justice likened the protests of a particular group to fighting words and of a personal character, and thus not protected speech. The majority disagreed and stated that the protester's speech was not personal but public, and that local laws which can shield individuals from protesters are adequate for protecting those in times of emotional distress.

I hear what you are saying, but trade is in the executive branch's wheelhouse. I saw this explanation on a discussion platform that I liked:

"The President, through the Trade Representative and through the Commerce Department, does have authority under Title 19 to change tariffs based on predefined conditions. The Supreme Court has upheld the imposition of tariffs imposed by the President where such tariffs were delegated by Congress to the President (something which I think is unconstitutional personally since a tariff is essentially a tax, but the Court found tariffs regulation essentially to be an act of foreign policy and interstate commerce).

The Commerce Department of the country and the Trade Representative are the primary organizations of the Executive Branch that implement national tariff policies. National tariff law is a hodgepodge of nonsense... Protecting some industries... Mandating others behave in certain ways... Etc... And it covers a span of time of tariffs from the 1850s to the 1990s. It's so complicated that the country has to publish what's called the "harmonized tariff and trade schedule" that is basically the summary version of what taxes are imposed on what industries...

Where a President might have a free hand is in cases where industries are allegedly suffering "market disruption" or in cases where safeguard measures are recommended... The President has tremendous authority under Title 19 to act. So for example, if companies are arguing that certain markets are non-functional, that domestic goods are being uniquely discriminated against in the marketplace, and that to safeguard industry something has to happen... The law empowers the President basically to take any action he sees fit in levying tariffs or other trade remedies against those markets. That power comes from these cases I mentioned earlier about Congress being able to delegate the power to the President. While the International Trade Commission would make its recommendations, and the Trade Representative would weigh in, and Commerce would weigh in, the President can more or less do what he wants...

There is a recent example of this type of action. In 2002, a former President imposed massive tariffs on steel imports into the country in order to safeguard the domestic steel industry from imminent collapse. While the international trade organization ultimately ruled those tariffs to be in violation of treaty obligations, and gave the power to another region to raise tariffs on domestic goods entering, the fact of the matter is the former President had the power... He used it... And when finally faced with retaliation, it was the former President who made the decision to end the tariffs... But by the time all that had wound its way through various legal machinations - he had accomplished what he wanted - he gave steel about five years to get its act together...

The mechanism usually used to do what a recent President is talking about are the provisions of the countervailing duties and/or the anti-dumping provisions of Title 19. That allows the President to essentially punish countries that favor their own goods versus domestic goods as well as remove the profit motive to sell goods in the country at way below the costs of production. The recent President could argue both of those with respect to certain imports... And probably successfully levy massive tariffs...

While ultimately the international trade organization would be a check against massive tariffs across the board... Those machinations take time. Just like in the steel case... If the recent President wanted to punish a certain country... He probably could for a period of time... Arguing that the countervailing tariffs were necessary to respond to currency manipulation. Would the country win that argument at the international trade organization? It might... But even if it doesn't... It would take years to sort out - and the other country would suffer in the meantime...

Honestly, however, I think the recent President's policies if enacted would likely start a trade war we haven't seen in nearly 100 years... And the international trade organization might collapse under the weight of it all..."
